lines.text: אדר 1
parenes brought from Mesopotamia to
Samaria, 2 K. 17, 31. b) A son of Sen-
nacherib king of Assyria, who aided in
slaying his father, Is. 37, 38. 2 K. 19, 37.
אֶדְרָע Chald. i. q. דְּרָע, the arm, with
א prosthetic, Ezra 4, 23. Hebr. זְרוֹעַ.
In the Targums with Patah אֶדְרַע.
Hence
אֶדְרֶעִי (strong, mighty) Edrei, pr. n.
a) The former metropolis of Bashan,
situated in the territory of Manasseh,
Called by Eusebius Ἀδραά, by Ptolemy
Ἄδρα, by Arabian geographers زرع
Zer’a, now درعا Der’â. [According to
Euseb. and the Peut. Tables, it lay 24
Rom. miles from Bozrah on the way to
Capitolias and Gadara. See Reland
Palæstina p. 547. Bibl. Res. in Pal. III.
App. p. 152.—R.] b) A city in Naph-
tali, Josh. 19, 37.
אַדֶּרֶת 1. Fem. of adj. אַדִּיר, large,
great, mighty, (comp. שַׁלִּיט, f. שַׁלֶּטֶת,)
Ez. 17, 8 גֶּפֶן אַדֶּרֶת a large vine, i. e. full
of branches and leaves. Comp. אַדִּיר
no. 1.
2. Subst. a wide cloak, mantle, pallium,
אַדֶּרֶת שִׁנְעָר a Babylonish mantle Josh. 7,
21, i. e. variegated with figures, having
the figures of men and animals interwo-
ven in colours; comp. Plin. H. N. 8. 48.
So אַדֶּרֶת שֵׂעָר a hairy mantle, shaggy
with hair, or (according to some) of fur,
3. splendour, glory, Zech. 11, 3.
* אָדַשׁ i. q. דּוּשׁ, to thresh, once inf.
absol. Is. 28, 28 אָדוֹשׁ יְדוּשֶׁנּוּ threshing
he threshes it.
* אָהַב and אָהֵב fut. יֶאֱהַב and יֶאְהַב,
1 pers. אֵהַב Prov. 8, 17 and אֹהַב Hos. 14,
5; inf. אֱהֹב Ecc. 3, 8, also אַהֲבָה q. v.
1. to breathe after, to long for, to de-
כִּי Ps. 116, 1.—This sense of breathing
after belongs to the syllables הב, חב,
and with the letters softened אב, או;
comp. the roots הָבַל; חָבַב, حَبَّ to de-
sire, to love; אָוָה and אָבָה to desire, to
be willing.
2. to love, in which signif. it is kindr.
17 אהה
with עָגַב, ἀγαπάω. With acc. Gen. 37,
3. 4. Deut. 4, 37; rarely c. לְ Lev. 19, 18.
17 אַהֲבַת נַפְשׁוֹ אֲהֵבוֹ he loved him as he
loved his own soul. Part. אֹהֵב a friend,
loving and beloved, intimate, different
from רֵעַ a companion, Prov. 18, 24. Esth.
5, 10. 14. Is. 41, 8 זֶרַע אַבְרָהָם אֹהֲבִי the
seed of Abraham my friend.
3. to love to do any thing, to delight
in doing, seq. infin. c. לְ, Hos. 12, 8 לַעֲשֹׁק
אָהֵב he loveth to oppress. Is. 56, 10. Jer.
Niph. part. נֶאֱהָב lovely, amiable, wor-
thy of love, 2 Sam. 1, 23.
Piel part. מְאַהֵב 1. a friend, Zech.
2. a lover, but only in a bad sense, a
paramour, debauchee, Ez. 16, 33 sq. 23,
5 sq. i. e. metaph. for an idolater.
Deriv. the three following.
אַהַב, only in plur. אֲהָבִים 1. loves,
spec. in a bad sense, amours, trop. of
intercourse and alliances with foreign
nations, Hos. 8, 9.
2. delight, loveliness. Prov. 5, 19 אַיֶּלֶת
אֲהָבִים a lovely hind.
אֹהַב m. love, in sing. once meton. for
lovers, paramours, Hos. 9, 10. Sept.
οἱ ἠγαπημένοι. Plur. אֲהָבִים loves, spec.
amours, Prov. 7, 18.
אַהֲבָה f. 1. Inf. fem. of the verb אָהַב,
with לְ pref. Is. 56, 6 לְאַהֲבָה אֶת־שֵׁם יְהֹוָה
to love the name of Jehovah. Deut. 10,
בְּ 1 K. 10, 9 בְּאַהֲבַת יְהֹוָה אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל in
Jehovah’s loving Israel, i. e. because he
loved Israel. In the same sense with
pref. כְּ Hos. 3, 1, and מִן Deut. 7, 8 מֵאַהֲבַת
יְהוָֹה אֶתְכֶם because Jehovah loved you.
2. love, espec. between the sexes, Cant.
2, 4. 5, 8. 8, 6. 7; of God towards men
Hos. 3, 1; of friends towards each other,
3. love, delight, concr. one beloved,
fem. Cant. 2, 7. 3, 5. So perh. v. 10,
where others as adv. lovely.
* אָהַד obsol. root, i. q. אָחַד to be one,
united. Hence אֵהוּד and
אֹהַד Ohad, pr. n. of a son of Simeon,

line_status.note: This is the running head: unpointed אדר centred, with the page number at the far right edge of the same line. A "1" is clearly printed there, followed by a second digit cut off by the crop edge (almost certainly "17"). Reading A omits the page number; B records the visible "1". No vowel points, dagesh or accents are printed on אדר.

Under the aleph of the final word three dots (segol) are printed, as in the headword אֶדְרָע on line 2; "with Patah" refers to the resh (רַע for רָע). Reading A wrongly gives patah under aleph; Reading B has the right vowels but inserts a space before the period, which is printed flush against the word.

The two readings differ only in the apostrophe glyph; the printed apostrophes in Zer’a and Der’â are typographic (curly ’), so Reading B matches. Arabic درعا and the circumflex â are identical in both and correct.

Decisive difference is the last word: the print shows segol (three dots) under the yod and a simple sheva (two vertical dots) under the aleph — יֶאְהַב — not sheva under yod with tsere under aleph as in B. The rest of the line is identical in both readings and matches the print.
First root begins with ה (visible gap between the left leg and the roof), unlike the closed ח of חָבַב next to it; all other points agree in both readings.
Under the aleph the print shows a shva followed by a short flat stroke (hataf-patah ֲ), not the T-shaped qamats of hataf-qamats ֳ; the qamats sits under the he. Reading B matches.

Under the ה of the final verb the print shows a single horizontal stroke (patach), not the two dots of tsere; so אָהַב (Reading B), not אָהֵב. The comma is also visibly set off from the word by a space, as in B.
The holam dot is printed over the vav (left of the he's upright), not over the he; vav carries holam + qamets, as in Reading B.
The printed word is plene with a vav bearing shureq (אֵהוּד, Ehud) and tsere under the aleph; Reading A's אֹהַד is the next line's Ohad, not this line's word.
